title: A demo menu — scripted walkthroughs that are simultaneously a tutorial, a review tool, and a real-server integration test
summary: A big, obvious button opening a menu of named demos (e.g. 'The GM Process'). Picking one runs a scripted, step-by-step macro against the REAL live module and the REAL local Foundry server — never mocked — narrating what a GM or player would do at each step and driving the actual UI to do it. Triples as: a tutorial for a new user, Ingram's fast lane to trying and critiquing a UI flow end to end, and a real-server test that anything broken breaks loudly during the demo itself.
description:
Ingram's own framing, captured close to verbatim (2026-09-17, mid-session on the deck rebuild): 'create a system for demos... a nice big obvious button to access a menu of possible demos... shows off how a UI element works by going through a macro that acts like a tutorial AND also allows me to experience your UI/UX work directly. Anything which breaks should break during the demo because we always run real commands on the real server to prove our process is a good one that works... a very long demo called "The GM Process" which shows how the GM would go through the story one step at a time and show off what the UI would help them do at each step... a tutorial and test AND a way for me to try out your ideas, critique them and then get the same experience again +/- my suggested changes. This allows us to walk through the entire experience of using the UI which gives me a fast track to debugging and helping design the UX.'

**Why this is more than a nice-to-have, and worth its own real design pass rather than a quick bolt-on:** it directly answers this session's own recurring cost — every UI change in this project currently gets verified by hand, one Browser-pane click sequence at a time, re-derived fresh each session (see reference_local_foundry_test_environment). A scripted, replayable demo is that same verification work, captured once and made replayable by anyone (Claude in a future session, or Ingram himself), AND it is the fastest possible loop for the exact iterative-review style already established as this project's working pattern (feedback_iterative_visual_review: get something real on screen, react to it in short terms, re-run to confirm the correction landed). 'Same experience again +/- my suggested changes' is literally re-running the demo after an edit — which this project already does by hand, constantly, throughout this very session.

**The 'never mocked' constraint is the load-bearing design decision.** A demo step is not a scripted animation or a canned screenshot — it is a real macro issuing real actions against the real live module and a real Foundry world (create/select a token, click the actual deck control, post the actual chat message, advance the actual day-ring setting), the same way this session's own live-verification passes already work, just captured as a replayable script instead of ad hoc tool calls. If a step's target element has moved, been renamed, or the underlying system has drifted, the demo throws or visibly stalls at exactly that step — which is the point: 'anything which breaks should break during the demo.'

**Relationship to existing testing tiers, worth being precise about:** design/testing-strategy.md's tiers (0-4) test CODE — pure logic, contracts, mocked adapters. This is a different, additive thing: a scripted END-TO-END walkthrough of USER-FACING FLOW, closer in spirit to the battle-simulator's real-dice, real-rules-engine philosophy (tools/battle-simulator/) than to a unit test, but for the UI instead of combat math. It would not replace any existing tier — a demo breaking tells you the FLOW broke, not which function; the existing tiers still own root-causing it once flagged.

**A concrete shape worth recording, not committing to:** a demo is a named, ordered list of steps, each step pairing (a) a narrated line of what a GM/player is doing and why, written in the GM-facing prose style this project already keeps to (feedback_gm_facing_prose_style — plain instructional sentences, no aphorism), and (b) the real action to perform (a DOM interaction on the real rendered deck, or a direct call to the same adapter function a click would trigger) plus what to check afterward before calling the step done. A menu (the 'big obvious button') lists demos by name; running one narrates each step, pauses or highlights the element in question (echoing 'shows off how a UI element works'), and only advances once the step's own check confirms the real state actually changed. Whether narration is passive (auto-advancing with a pause) or Ingram clicks 'next' himself is an open question below, as is whether steps are skippable/replayable individually rather than only as one continuous run.

**Not started.** Ingram was explicit: capture this as a tracked objective, do not build it now. This entry exists so it is not rediscovered from scratch whenever it does become the right thing to pick up.
sourceContext: Mid-session on the deck rebuild, immediately after a round of live UI feedback (grime tuning, hiding the native player roster, the hotbar rampart, the scene-runner drawer). Ingram explicitly said not to implement yet and to track it as an objective for whenever it seems best to start.
openSubQuestions: Where does a demo script actually live — hand-authored JS per demo (closest to how this session's own live verification calls already read), or a small declarative step format (narration + selector + action + assertion) that a shared runner interprets? The declarative shape is more reusable and more reviewable by Ingram without reading code, but is real design work of its own — a mini DSL — not something to default into.

Auto-advancing narration with a pause between steps, or GM-paced (a 'Next' click per step, matching how Ingram already prefers to review UI work — feedback_iterative_visual_review says he reacts to something real on screen, which argues for pacing HE controls)?

Does a demo run against the shared local test world (bi-console-test), or does it need its own disposable throwaway world per run so a half-finished demo never leaves stray state (a posted chat message, an advanced day-ring, a granted artefact) sitting in the world Ingram actually uses for other testing?

Can a demo's own steps be skipped to / replayed individually once authored, or is a demo strictly one continuous run start to finish? 'Get the same experience again +/- my suggested changes' argues for cheap re-running of the WHOLE thing at minimum; per-step replay is a nice-to-have on top, not assumed.

How much of 'The GM Process' (the worked example named directly) would double-cover ground design/scene-simulation-testing.md's self-play protocol (issue #137) already covers from a different angle — that protocol predicts outcomes and cross-checks against a live UI run too. Worth reading that doc first when this is picked up, to reuse rather than duplicate its own real-server-verification discipline.

Does a broken demo step get filed as a GitHub issue automatically (matching feedback_github_tracker_discipline's 'log it in the same turn' rule), or does surfacing it live to Ingram in the moment count as the loud failure the design already wants?
